candidate.answerReason: Constructing an inner regular hexagon and subtracting six circular segments gives \(3\sqrt{3}-\pi\), agreeing with choice D.

methods.label: An inner hexagon minus six circular segments
methods.explanation:
The intersections of neighboring arcs suggest constructing a smaller hexagon. Let \(O\) be the center of the original hexagon. Joining \(O\) to its vertices produces six equilateral triangles of side \(2\). Mark the midpoint of each segment joining \(O\) to a vertex. These six midpoints form a regular hexagon of side \(1\), by the triangle midsegment theorem.

Consider an original side \(AB\). Let \(P,Q\) be the midpoints of \(OA,OB\), respectively, and let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\). The midsegment theorem gives
\[
MP=MQ=PQ=1.
\]
Thus \(P\) and \(Q\) lie on the semicircle with diameter \(AB\). The trapezoid \(ABQP\) is contained in that semicircle: its four vertices lie on the circle, and it lies on the inward side of \(AB\). The six such trapezoids cover everything between the original and smaller hexagons.

Inside the smaller hexagon, this semicircle removes the circular segment bounded by \(PQ\) and the inward arc from \(P\) to \(Q\). This segment lies in triangle \(OPQ\). Indeed, each bordering radial line meets the circle only at its original vertex and its midpoint, and only the midpoint lies on the inner side of \(PQ\). Consequently the segment cannot cross either bordering line. The six removed segments therefore have disjoint interiors.

Since triangle \(MPQ\) is equilateral, its central angle at \(M\) is \(60^\circ\). A unit equilateral triangle has height \(\sqrt{1-(1/2)^2}=\sqrt3/2\), so its area is \(\sqrt3/4\). Each circular segment consequently has area
\[
\frac{60}{360}\pi-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}
=\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}.
\]
The smaller hexagon consists of six unit equilateral triangles. Hence the shaded area is
\[
6\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}
-6\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)
=\boxed{3\sqrt3-\pi},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

methods.label: Correct for overlapping semicircles
methods.explanation:
Each semicircle has radius \(1\), so their areas sum to \(3\pi\). To subtract their union from the hexagon, we must account for the overlaps.

Let \(O\) be the hexagon's center. Its six central triangles are equilateral with side \(2\), so their heights are \(\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3\). Therefore the six side midpoints, which are the semicircle centers, form a regular hexagon with center-to-vertex distance \(\sqrt3\). Dropping perpendiculars in its central triangles shows that centers two positions apart are distance \(3\) apart; opposite centers are distance \(2\sqrt3\) apart. Both distances exceed \(2\). Such semicircles cannot overlap, because a point in two unit disks would put their centers at distance at most \(1+1=2\).

Thus only neighboring semicircles overlap. Also, no point belongs to three semicircles, since any three centers include a nonadjacent pair.

Consider two neighboring semicircles meeting at an original vertex \(V\), and call their centers \(M,N\). Let \(P\) be the midpoint of \(OV\). Since \(OV=2\), we have \(VP=1\). Applying the midsegment theorem in the two central triangles beside \(OV\) gives \(MP=NP=1\). Hence both triangles \(MVP\) and \(NVP\) are equilateral. The overlap is the lens bounded by the inward arcs from \(V\) to \(P\), each subtending \(60^\circ\). Its area is
\[
2\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)
=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
There are exactly six neighboring pairs. Adding all semicircle areas counts each lens twice and every other covered point once, so adding each lens back once corrects the subtraction. The original hexagon has area \(6\sqrt3\), giving shaded area
\[
6\sqrt3-3\pi
+6\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)
=\boxed{3\sqrt3-\pi}.
\]
The answer is \(\mathrm{D}\).
